lead: A tendon is jacked to a chosen force, but that force does not stay. The concrete shortens, the tendon rubs on its duct, the wedges draw in, and over the years the concrete creeps and shrinks while the steel relaxes. Each effect removes part of the jacking force P<sub>0</sub>; what is left is the effective prestress P<sub>e</sub>, typically 75 to 85 percent of P<sub>0</sub>. The service checks of every prestressed member use P<sub>e</sub>, so the losses must be worked out, not guessed.
prereq: You need the properties of the two materials (Es, Ec, creep, shrinkage, relaxation) and the two stressing systems.

head: Loss
Pre-tensioned
Post-tensioned
When
rows: only when tendons are stressed one after another

blocks.text: Each loss is a loss of tendon stress Δf in N/mm²; multiply by Ap in mm² for a force in N, then divide by 1000 for kN. Everything below is for a bonded tendon whose strain follows the concrete at its level.
Elastic shortening. At transfer the concrete at tendon level is compressed to fc and shortens by fc/Ec; the tendon shortens with it.
Δf<sub>es</sub> = m f<sub>c</sub>,   f<sub>c</sub> = P<sub>i</sub>/A + P<sub>i</sub> e²/I
blocks.where: m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub>; f<sub>c</sub> is the concrete stress at tendon level in N/mm² (the self-weight term M<sub>g</sub>e/I can be subtracted when the question gives it); P<sub>i</sub> in N, e in mm, I in mm⁴.

blocks.text: In a post-tensioned member stressed with one jack, the first tendon loses force as each later tendon squeezes the concrete, and the last loses nothing. With n tendons the average loss is (n − 1)/(2n) of m f<sub>c</sub>, which many textbooks round to half.

Friction. A tendon pulled through a curved duct presses on the duct wall and rubs (curvature friction, coefficient μ); small unintended wiggles of the duct add wobble friction (coefficient k per metre):

blocks.where: P<sub>x</sub> is the force at x metres from the jack; α is the total angle change of the tendon over that length in radians; for a parabola of sag e and span L, α = 8e/L over the full span; e in the exponent is the base 2.718. μ and k come from the code or the duct supplier.

blocks.text: Anchorage slip. At lock-off the wedges draw in by δ, usually 3 to 6 mm. If friction is negligible the whole tendon length L shortens uniformly and Δf = Esδ/L. With friction, the draw-in is resisted by reverse friction and is used up over a setting length ls from the anchor: ls = √(EsApδ/p), where p is the friction loss of force per unit length. The force loss is 2pls at the anchor, falling to zero at ls. The uniform formula then badly understates the loss at the jack end.
Δf<sub>cr</sub> = φ m f<sub>c</sub>    Δf<sub>sh</sub> = ε<sub>sh</sub> E<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: φ is the creep coefficient (ultimate creep strain divided by elastic strain); ε<sub>sh</sub> is the shrinkage strain after transfer. Textbook problems on IS 1343 commonly take φ = 2.2, 1.6 and 1.1 for loading at 7 days, 28 days and one year; ε<sub>sh</sub> = 300 × 10⁻⁶ for pre-tensioning and 200 × 10⁻⁶/log<sub>10</sub>(t + 2) for post-tensioning, t being the age in days at transfer. The 2012 code gives fuller tables by humidity and member size.

blocks.text: Relaxation is taken from the code table or the maker's test as a percentage of the initial stress; it rises steeply with initial stress, which is one reason the jacking stress is capped. Add all the stress losses, subtract from the initial stress, and multiply by Ap to get Pe. A rough first design may take total losses as 15 to 20 percent for post-tensioning and 20 to 25 percent for pre-tensioning, but an exam problem expects each loss computed.

examples.question: A pre-tensioned beam 200 mm × 300 mm has 320 mm² of wires stressed to 1200 N/mm², at 50 mm below the centroid. E<sub>s</sub> = 210 kN/mm², E<sub>c</sub> = 35 kN/mm², creep coefficient 1.6, shrinkage strain 300 × 10⁻⁶ and relaxation 3 percent of the initial stress. Ignore the self-weight. Find each loss, the total percentage loss and the effective force.
examples.answer: Losses: elastic shortening 51.2, creep 81.9, shrinkage 63 and relaxation 36 N/mm², total 232.1 N/mm² (19.3 percent); P<sub>e</sub> = 309.7 kN from 384 kN.

examples.question: A post-tensioned girder of span 20 m has a parabolic tendon (A<sub>p</sub> = 1000 mm²) with its ends at the centroid and a sag of 400 mm. It is jacked from one end to 1200 kN. μ = 0.30, k = 0.0020 per m, wedge draw-in 5 mm, E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm². Find the force at the far end after friction, the setting length and the force at the jack end after lock-off.
steps: Far-end force P<sub>L</sub> = 1200 × 0.9158 = 1,098.9 kN, a friction loss of 101.1 kN (8.4 percent).
Friction loss per unit length p ≈ 101.1/20 = 5.054 kN/m = 5.054 N/mm.
Setting length l<sub>s</sub> = √(195,000 × 1000 × 5/5.054) = 13,889 mm = 13.89 m, less than 20 m, so the draw-in does not reach the far end.
Loss at the jack end = 2pl<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 5.054 × 13.89 = 140.4 kN; force there after lock-off = 1200 − 140.4 = 1,059.6 kN.
For comparison, the uniform formula E<sub>s</sub>δ/L gives 195,000 × 5/20,000 = 48.75 N/mm², only 48.8 kN: too small near the anchor.
examples.answer: After friction the far end has 1,098.9 kN. The 5 mm draw-in is absorbed within 13.89 m and leaves 1,059.6 kN at the jack end; beyond 13.89 m the friction curve stands.

traps: Using degrees in μα. Convert to radians; α for a parabola over the full span is 8e/L.
Charging a post-tensioned member with full elastic shortening when all tendons are stressed together. Then the loss is nil; for one-by-one stressing it is (n − 1)/(2n) of m f<sub>c</sub>.
Using E<sub>s</sub>δ/L for draw-in on a long curved tendon. With friction the loss is 2pl<sub>s</sub> at the anchor.
Swapping creep and relaxation: creep belongs to the concrete, relaxation to the steel.
Using P<sub>0</sub> in the service check. Use P<sub>e</sub> after all losses.

quiz.q: List the losses of prestress in a pre-tensioned member.
quiz.a: Elastic shortening, creep and shrinkage of concrete, and relaxation of steel (plus a small slip at the bed grips). There is no duct friction.

quiz.q: Write the friction formula and define each term.
quiz.a: P<sub>x</sub> = P<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−(μα + kx)</sup>: P<sub>0</sub> jacking force, μ curvature friction coefficient, α angle change in radians, k wobble coefficient per metre, x distance from the jack in metres.

quiz.q: Why is shrinkage loss smaller in a post-tensioned member?
quiz.a: The concrete is older when it is stressed, so part of its shrinkage has already happened before the tendon is anchored; the formula 200 × 10⁻⁶/log<sub>10</sub>(t + 2) falls as t grows.

quiz.q: Find the shrinkage loss in a post-tensioned beam stressed at 14 days, E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm².
Four tendons are stressed one after another in a beam where m = 6 and the final concrete stress at tendon level is 7 N/mm². Find the average elastic shortening loss.
quiz.a: (n − 1)/(2n) × m f<sub>c</sub> = 3/8 × 6 × 7 = 15.75 N/mm². The first tendon loses 3/4 × 42 = 31.5 N/mm², the last none.

quiz.q: In the second worked example, the tendon is jacked from both ends instead. What changes?
quiz.a: The force is lowest at midspan instead of at the far end: there μα + kx = 0.30 × 0.08 + 0.0020 × 10 = 0.044, so P = 1200 × 0.957 = 1,148.3 kN instead of 1,098.9 kN. Draw-in happens at both ends, so both end zones lose force, but the loss at midspan is roughly halved.

quiz.q: Why is adding all losses as fixed percentages of P<sub>0</sub> only a first estimate?
quiz.a: The losses interact: creep depends on the concrete stress, which itself falls as the other losses occur; friction varies along the tendon; relaxation depends on the stress that remains. A design computes each from the actual stresses at the section being checked.

beyond: Not for the exam. On large bridges, load cells at a few anchorages and vibrating-wire strain gauges in the concrete track the real loss over the years. Time-step programs compute creep, shrinkage and relaxation together in small steps. Search for prestress loss monitoring and age-adjusted effective modulus.

figure.caption: Tendon force along the 20 m girder of the second worked example. Friction lowers it from 1200 kN at the jack to 1098.9 kN at the far end; the 5 mm draw-in then lowers the jack end to 1059.6 kN, and its effect dies out 13.89 m from the jack.
